meta.title: Who really said "Yesterday's home runs don't win today's games"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No documented source in Babe Ruth's own words has been found. Wikiquote lists it as disputed: a similar maxim circulated as unattributed folk wisdom by 1959, and the Ruth credit starts in the 1980s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Yesterday's home runs don't win today's games'?
meta.ogDescription: Babe Ruth gets the credit, but no documented source has him saying it. Wikiquote files it as disputed folk wisdom — a similar maxim in print by 1959, attributed to Ruth only decades later.

answer.label: Not Babe Ruth — an anonymous baseball proverb
answer.authorDates: A similar maxim in print by 1959 · credited to Babe Ruth only from the 1980s
answer.sourceLine: No documented source in Babe Ruth’s own words has been found — no book, interview or newspaper report that we or Wikiquote can point to has Ruth (1895–1948) saying it. The Wikiquote entry for Babe Ruth ↗ files the line under Disputed, noting that the earliest similar wordings appear as unattributed folk wisdom — its example being a February 1959 piece that quotes the maxim “yesterday’s home-run doesn’t count in today’s game” with no speaker attached — and that the Ruth credit does not begin until the 1980s.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the proverb predates the attribution, and the attribution rests on no source at all.

trail: Nothing at Quote Investigator. A search of quoteinvestigator.com ↗ returns no matching article, so the specialist anchor here is Wikiquote.

Wikiquote calls it disputed. The Babe Ruth entry ↗ lists the line under Disputed, gives a February 1959 example of the maxim circulating as unattributed folk wisdom, and states the Ruth attribution begins only in the 1980s.
Absent from the sourced collections. It is not among the citation-bearing quotations at Baseball Almanac ↗, and does not appear in the SABR biography by Allan Wood ↗.
Modern databases repeat it without a source. The Goodreads entry ↗ credits Ruth with no book, date or interview, and flags its own quotations as community-added and unverified.
source.excerptNote: This 1959 sentence is not by Babe Ruth and does not name him. It is quoted here as Wikiquote transcribes it, from F. N. Abbott’s “On Your Marks” in a fraternity magazine — the earliest similar wording that page documents. The scan Wikiquote links is on HathiTrust and could not be opened for independent confirmation, so this detail rests on Wikiquote’s citation rather than on our own reading of the page.
source.rightsNote: We cannot assert a rights status. The popular wording has no identified author or first publication — it circulates as an anonymous proverb, and the only documented earlier appearance is a differently worded 1959 magazine line whose authorship and status we did not independently verify. Because we cannot tie this exact sentence to a specific work, we make no public-domain claim.

author.heading: About Babe Ruth
author.metaLine: 1895–1948 · American baseball player, Boston Red Sox, New York Yankees & Boston Braves
author.bio: George Herman “Babe” Ruth played 22 major-league seasons from 1914 to 1935, converting from a dominant left-handed pitcher into the hitter who reshaped baseball around the home run. He finished with the Boston Braves in 1935, playing his last major-league game on 30 May that year. His fame is precisely the problem: a name that famous attracts unsourced aphorisms. The Baseball Almanac collection of Ruth quotations, which cites books and interviews for many of its entries, does not contain this line at all — and neither does the Society for American Baseball Research biography of him.

misattribution.heading: How the Babe got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a proverb that acquired a celebrity, not a celebrity line that got shortened. Each stage of the drift is documented on the same page.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ places the line in its Disputed section and states that the quote “does not begin to be attributed to Babe Ruth until the 1980s.” Ruth died in 1948.

Wikiquote’s cited 1959 example carries the maxim in a different shape — a home run that “doesn’t count” rather than one that “doesn’t win” — and presents it as a saying to be remembered, with no speaker attached ↗.
The line is missing from the citation-bearing Baseball Almanac Ruth quotation page ↗ and from the SABR biography of Ruth ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Best available finding: an anonymous baseball proverb, in print in a related form by 1959, retro-fitted to Babe Ruth decades later — as documented by Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to Ruth
lead: The line works as a Babe Ruth quote because it sounds like one. It is about home runs, it is about not coasting, and Ruth is the most home-run-shaped figure in American sport — so the sentence and the name fit together with no friction. That fit is exactly what makes the attribution untestable by ear, and why it has to be tested against documents instead.

Against documents, it fails. Wikiquote’s Babe Ruth page places it in the Disputed section, notes the earliest similar wordings circulating as unattributed folk wisdom, and observes that the Ruth credit only starts appearing in the 1980s. The proverb, in other words, existed as a saying before anyone put a famous mouth behind it.
detailsBody: The maxim also travels in more than one shape — the familiar “yesterday’s home runs don’t win today’s games” and, in the 1959 appearance Wikiquote cites, “yesterday’s home-run doesn’t count in today’s game.” Unstable wording across variants is a normal signature of proverbial folk speech rather than a remembered utterance by a specific person.

Modern quote databases reproduce the Ruth credit without documentation. The Goodreads entry ↗ carries no book, date, or interview, and the site itself notes that its quotations are community-added and unverified.
context.pull: The saying came first. The famous name was added later.
